## Root causes — three stories behind fifteen classes

Most of the classes below are not independent bugs; they are one of three
systemic, architectural differences between the two harnesses, each surfacing
once per ADMIT rule it touches. Read this section before the class list.

**1. The C# harness gates `canonicalize`/`canonicalize_nfc` through the full ADMIT
parser; the Rust harness does not.** `tools/Curia.Differential/Program.cs`'s
`Canonicalize()` always calls `JsonReader.Parse` — the *same* function `admit`
uses, enforcing every ADMIT business rule (size, depth, member count, string
length, duplicate keys, non-finite numbers, noncharacters) — before ever calling
`CanonicalJson.Canonicalize`/`CanonicalizeWithNfc`. `rust/curia-testis/src/bin/
curia-differential.rs`'s dispatch calls `curia_testis::canonicalize`/
`canonicalize_with_nfc` directly — both use the bare RFC 8259 `json::parse`,
never `json::admit`. The result: for *any* document that is syntactically valid
JSON but violates an ADMIT-only rule, C# rejects (propagating the ADMIT slug)
while Rust accepts and canonicalizes it. This alone accounts for the
depth-exceeded, members-exceeded, string-too-long, noncharacter, and
raw-duplicate-key classes below, on both `canonicalize` and `canonicalize_nfc`.

**2. `admit`'s own number-safety rule (R6.33/errata D5, integer-only,
±(2^53-1)) is applied universally by Rust's `admit()` but not applied at all by
the generic `JsonReader` this harness's C# `admit`/`canonicalize`/
`canonicalize_nfc` ops share.** `JsonReader.ReadNumber` (`src/Curia.Canon/Json/
JsonReader.cs`) checks only `double.IsFinite`; `check_number`
(`rust/curia-testis/src/json.rs`) checks integer-ness and the safe range on
*every* number in the tree, not a rule scoped to one envelope field. Whether
this Rust-side check is meant to be that general, or scoped to a specific field
(e.g. an envelope's `meta_prediction`) the way `R6.33`'s example implies, is a
spec question this report does not adjudicate — only the code-level divergence
is reported here. Because number values are untouched by NFC normalization, this
one shows up only on `admit`, never on `canonicalize`/`canonicalize_nfc`.

**3. `CanonicalizeWithNfc` (C#) has no defense against an NFC-manufactured
duplicate key; `canonicalize_with_nfc` (Rust) does.** Two wire-distinct member
names that collide only after NFC normalization (e.g. precomposed vs. combining-
sequence "café") are silently rendered as two members sharing one key by
`CanonicalJson.cs`'s `NormalizeToNfc`+`Write` (not valid I-JSON — a re-parse
could pick either member, so two verifiers checking the same signature over the
same canonical bytes could disagree about what was actually said). Rust's
`nfc.rs` has a dedicated two-pass check for exactly this ("Fix rounds 1-3" in its
own doc comments) and rejects with `curia/canon/duplicate-normalized-key`. Of
every finding in this report, this is the one with the most direct bearing on
P22 (envelope inseparability) and signature non-repudiation: it means the C#
`CanonicalizeWithNfc` path can be made to emit invalid, ambiguous canonical
bytes from validly-ADMITted input, silently.

**Not part of either pattern**, and each its own independent, narrower finding:
the three ADMIT slug-*naming* mismatches (`size-exceeded`/`too-large`,
`members-exceeded`/`too-many-members`, `malformed`/`malformed-json` — the
already-known divergence this task specifically expected); the raw-control-
character slug C# has no dedicated name for; the unpaired-surrogate class where
C#/Rust both reject but the node oracle silently accepts (substituting U+FFFD —
see "Node oracle quirk" below); and the `duplicate-key`-vs-`malformed-json` class,
which is a check-*order* divergence, not a check-*presence* one: C#'s single-pass
`Utf8JsonReader` notices a raw duplicate key the moment it reads the second
occurrence's property name, mid-parse; Rust checks duplicates only in `admit()`'s
tree walk, which runs strictly *after* a complete, successful `json::parse` — so
on a document that is both duplicate-keyed *and* truncated before that duplicate
key's value, C# reports the duplicate (found first) and Rust reports the
truncation (parse never completes, so the duplicate check never runs).

**Node oracle quirk (informational, not a divergence under the stated rules):**
the generator's own report flagged this and this run confirms it — `oracle.mjs`'s
hand-rolled `\u` decoding builds a JS string containing an unpaired surrogate
rather than rejecting it, which `Buffer.from(str,'utf8')` then silently converts
to U+FFFD. That is why the `canonicalize/mixed-result::csharp-fail::rust-fail::
node-ok` class exists (667 occurrences, the single largest class by volume) —
C# and Rust correctly agree in rejecting every one of these, and node is the
odd one out. Per the task's comparison rule, "all three fail or all three
succeed" for `canonicalize`, and node is authoritative on RFC 8785 disagreements
— but an unpaired surrogate is not a pure-RFC-8785 question at all (RFC 8785
has nothing to say about invalid input), so this is reported as its own class
rather than silently deferred to node.

## Supplemental cases

Hand-constructed cases prepended to the generated corpus, each documented at its
definition site in `compare.mjs` (`buildSupplementalCases`). Included because the
property-driven generator (`generate.mjs`) has no category that reaches them:

- `size-exceeded` — a document over the 1 MiB overall submission-size cap; no
  generator category produces a document anywhere near this size (the largest
  generated documents are the 256 KiB *string*-cap cases).
- `malformed-generic` — the single byte `!`, a minimal generic JSON syntax error.
- `raw-control-character` — a raw (unescaped) control byte inside a string that is
  not NUL; found via source review, confirmed by direct invocation before inclusion.
- `non-integer-number` / `unsafe-integer` — deterministic instances of the ADMIT
  integer-safety rule (see the corresponding divergence class above); the generator's
  `numbers` category reaches this condition too, but only probabilistically.
- `duplicate-key-pure-canonicalize` / `nfc-collision-duplicate-key` — deterministic
  instances of the two duplicate-key divergences (see above); the generator's
  `admit-reject-boundary` category (`dup-identical`/`dup-nfc` kinds) reaches these too,
  but only probabilistically.
